text: I’ll model the leak path as a thin helical ribbon between two parallel 30° trapezoidal-thread flanks. The stated data do not define the trapezoid angle, so I am assuming the standard metric trapezoidal included angle of 30°. The 0.2 mm clearance is taken normal to the flank. I’ll close the ribbon at the thread root and crest with two additional named wall patches, then use a structured hexahedral mesh aligned with the helix. First I’m defining and viewing a coarse six-turn surface.

The preview shows the intended open-ended six-turn ribbon without turn-to-turn overlap. I’ll now discretize its boundary consistently from one structured grid and export all six surface patches together in the sense of a single shared triangulation; this prevents cracks between STL patch seams. The requested four patches remain distinct, while `threadRoot` and `threadCrest` close the two narrow radial edges.

I’m correcting every surface winding against its actual adjacent cell (important because Cartesian coordinates alone do not reveal which of the six turns a point belongs to), then using those same quads as the boundary of the coarse hexahedral volume mesh.
The coarse mesh is written. I’ll run the binding OpenFOAM mesh check now; if it passes, I’ll inspect the actual volume mesh rather than only the analytic preview.
The mesh itself was not read because this geometry-only case still needs a minimal `system/controlDict`. I’ll add only that required case metadata, then rerun the check separately.
With the case metadata present, I’m rerunning the binding check on the coarse mesh.
This OpenFOAM build also requires empty finite-volume dictionaries even for `checkMesh`. I’ll add those utility prerequisites without defining any solver or boundary conditions.
I’ll now run the coarse mesh check again.

All geometry metrics are good, but `checkMesh` reports the internal face list is not in OpenFOAM’s preferred upper-triangular ordering. This is addressing order, not bad cells. I’ll sort internal faces by owner and neighbour and rewrite the addressing while leaving the geometry unchanged.
I’ll verify that the addressing correction clears the mesh check.

The coarse mesh passes. I’ll now render the actual boundary quads and mesh lines, highlighting the two requested end patches, to confirm the meshed topology follows the analytic helix and remains open only at its two ends.

The inspected mesh has the right connected helical topology and clean end patches. For the final mesh I’ll double the circumferential resolution and increase resolution through both the 1 mm flank depth and the 0.2 mm clearance, giving 9,216 helix-aligned hexahedra. This also reduces the coarse mesh’s 13:1 maximum aspect ratio. The final STL files will be overwritten from the refined boundary so they continue to match the mesh exactly.
The refined mesh and matching STLs are written. I’ll run the binding check on the final mesh and report its quality figures.
